items.title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
items.desc: Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions. They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets. Continue reading...

items.title: What we learned from the government’s latest release of Mandelson documents
items.desc: From attempted influence on Starmer’s 2025 reshuffle to refusing to sell shares in a lobbying firm, here are some of the key points UK politics live – latest updates The government has published 32 new documents about Peter Mandelson’s appointment and tenure as British ambassador to Washington. This is the third tranche of papers since a parliamentary motion, known as a humble address, in February 2026 for “all papers” relevant to be released. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. items.desc: Timms review tackles some big questions about a flawed system – but leaves other issues in the ‘maybe later’ drawer Stephen Timms would be forgiven for feeling his thunder has been stolen. But when Timms took to the House of Commons to call for a “fundamental overhaul” of Pip on Tuesday, it was clear these were altogether bigger – and notably not explicitly cost-saving – ideas.
